title: Why Teachers HATE Professional Development
author: Spivey, Matt
summary: This piece is a pointed critique of how professional development is typically run, arguing that most PD wastes teachers' time on low-value busywork (poster paper, Post-It note activities, app-of-the-month engagement gimmicks) rather than substantive instructional content. The author's authority comes from having volunteered to run PD sessions himself as an English professor, motivated partly by genuine expertise transfer across content areas and partly, in his own framing, as 'an act of mercy' to spare colleagues from less useful sessions. His implicit standard for good PD is content that raises the whole institution's ethos toward rigor and high standards, not generic engagement tactics or redundant LMS updates that could have been communicated in an email. The piece functions as both complaint and prescription: it names exactly what makes PD hated (time-wasting, condescending activities, information that didn't need a live session) and gestures at the alternative — session content substantial enough to be 'interesting, challenging, and respectful' of the audience's expertise and time.
points: Diagnoses the core complaint about PD precisely: much of it delivers information that could have been an email, wrapped in busywork like poster-paper activities.
Frames good PD content as something that should be 'interesting, challenging, and respectful' of an expert audience's time, not a one-size-fits-all engagement gimmick.
Positions himself as running PD partly out of mercy — better a colleague delivers useful material than another generic 'get out of your seats' session.
Calls specifically for PD sessions to raise institutional standards and rigor, not push another app or an LMS update nobody will use.
quotes: Most PD is a complete waste of time, leaving teachers thinking to themselves, 'There's so much more I could be doing to help my students than this pointless activity forcing us to write on poster paper.'
And if there's anything of actual importance, it could have been an email instead of a four-hour PowerPoint presentation.

I knew I could present such useful material in a way that other professors would find interesting, challenging, and respectful of their time. Better me than the education professor who wanted them to get out of their seats and stick Post-It notes on the wall.

In this episode, I discuss some of the topics I used to discuss during these professional development meetings — how I tried not only to improve reading and writing on my campus, but to elevate the entire university ethos toward rigor and high standards.

Stop wasting teachers' time with yet another talk about a stupid new app teachers should download to improve student 'engagement' or an irrelevant update to the LMS no one will actually use. Get to the point. Say something truly valuable. And aim high.
